author: BBC News
description:
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said that “all the options will be on the table" as the government considers the future relationship with the European Union.
 
This comes after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.
 
Miliband also said that a deal agreed between the UK and the EU on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement.
 
The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.

author: BBC News
description:
Artificial intelligence is beginning to do something remarkable: teach itself. What once sounded like science fiction is now being taken seriously by some of the world's leading AI researchers. 

Could self-improving AI spark a new golden age of scientific discovery, helping humanity cure disease, grow replacement organs, tackle pollution and even uncover laws of nature that have so far remained beyond our reach? Or are we creating systems that could eventually improve themselves faster than humans can understand or control?

Joining AI Decoded is Richard Socher, co-founder and CEO of Recursive and author of The Eureka Machine. He explains his vision for a new generation of AI systems capable of accelerating scientific breakthroughs by learning from vast amounts of data, designing experiments and continually improving their own capabilities. Could these "Eureka Machines" become the greatest tool humanity has ever created?

Putting that vision to the test are AI Decoded co-hosts Priya
title: AI that builds itself: Golden age or time to panic? | BBC News

author: BBC News
description:
Could AI help save lives by giving communities more warning of dangerous landslides and debris flows?
 
Tech Now's Yasmin Morgan-Griffiths meets scientists in the Swiss Alps who are testing cutting-edge sensors, including a 2km, fibre-optic cable, to better understand how debris flows behave.
 
The data is being used in AI-powered early warning systems that could detect dangerous flows faster, potentially giving communities more time to evacuate.
 
The research comes as climate change increases the threat of landslides and avalanches around the world.

author: BBC News
description:
The internet is full of other people’s relationships. But how much of the advice out there is actually reliable? What are people being told online, and what impact is it having on their real-life relationships? 

In this episode of Top Comment, Marianna and Matt iron out what Cuffing season and Breadcrumbing mean, so you don't have to. 

They discuss how more psychological and clinical terms such as Attachment Theory and Narcissist are being simplified and used incorrectly, at times to sell products. 

And they hear from researchers and creators on how the algorithmic effect can lead you down a rabbit hole of labelling yourself and others.

author: BBC News
description:
After a week of tech chaos with flights grounded, plus outages at Microsoft, Apple, US banks, and the National Security Agency, questions continue to be asked about the cause of the disruption and whether it’s more than a series of coincidences.  Now the government’s top cyber security official, Sean Cairncross, is leaving his post, with CBS reporting he was fired.

Trump says these were “individual events”. But Republican Senator Josh Hawley says if it is all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world”. So who’s right?
In this episode, Sarah, Marianna and Anthony discuss the doubts over the official explanation, cuts to America’s cyber defences, and whether people trust what they’re being told by the White House. 

Plus, Sarah talks to the cybersecurity and cyberespionage expert Dmitri Alperovitch about the fall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and the race with China over AI chips. Are rushed fixes for problems found by AI behind the disruption?
